# What the man in the corner of the near court is there for

## Short answer

He is **security** — a member of the event's protective/crowd-control detail, posted at the corner of the empty court that separates the audience from the stage. He is **not** a tennis official of any kind. No tennis is being played: the courts have been turned into the floor of a political rally, so he is there to watch the crowd, hold the line at the corner where the stands meet the court, keep that empty court clear, and stop anyone from walking onto the floor or getting near the candidate.

## What the video actually shows

The clip is a shaky, hand-held phone video shot from high in the stands of an outdoor tennis stadium at night. Key details that establish the context:

- The stage set up on the far court is a **blue lectern reading "RON PAUL"**, flanked by loudspeakers on stands, with press photographers, campaign staff and a small standing press pen crowded around it.
- The back windscreens carry a row of **Pac-12 university logos** (Stanford's "S", Cal's script, a Washington "W", etc.) and a banner with a **bear** on it — this is UCLA's Los Angeles Tennis Center (Straus Stadium), the venue for Ron Paul's town-hall rally of 4 April 2012.
- Every seat in the stands is full and people are packed into the aisles and standing on the walkways — a capacity/overflow crowd of roughly six thousand. In the last few seconds of the clip the camera pans off the court to the area outside the gates, where **uniformed police officers stand in a line** holding back hundreds more people who could not get in. That confirms a heavy, layered security operation around the event.
- Critically, **there is no net in play, no players, no ball, no scoreboard in use and no match**. The nearest court is completely bare blue asphalt.

## The man himself, and why he is where he is

Zooming in on him (he sits/stands alone at the corner of the near court, at roughly the point where the blue surface meets the green apron in front of the front row) shows a man in a **dark suit with a white shirt**, hands held together in front of him, essentially motionless for the whole 20-odd seconds the court is on screen. He is one of **several identically dressed men spaced around the perimeter of that same empty court** — I can pick out at least three more: one at the left corner by the bleacher steps, one standing at the crowd barrier in the middle, and one at the right-hand edge in front of the stands.

His purpose is therefore:

1. **To guard the empty buffer court.** The near court has been deliberately left vacant as a stand-off zone between the packed spectators and the candidate's stage. Somebody has to be physically present to keep it empty, and he is the man assigned to the corner nearest the camera.
2. **To face the crowd rather than the speaker.** Throughout the clip he looks back toward the spectators, not toward the lectern — the standard posture of a protective detail, scanning the audience for anyone who might rush the stage, throw something, or cause a disturbance. Everyone else in the venue is looking at Ron Paul; he is looking at everyone else.
3. **To plug the most likely breach point.** He is stationed exactly at the corner where the low barrier/fencing, the aisle steps and the front row of seating all meet the court surface — the easiest place for a spectator to step down onto the floor. He functions as a human checkpoint at that gap.
4. **To be part of a continuous cordon.** Because he is one of a ring of similarly posted guards, his individual job is to cover his own arc of the perimeter so that the whole boundary between the crowd and the stage is watched without gaps.
5. **Incidentally, to keep sightlines and exits controlled** — he also keeps people from spilling out of the jammed aisles onto the court, which matters at an event the fire marshal had already capped.

## What he is *not*

- He is **not a chair umpire** — the umpire's chair sits at the middle of the net, not in a corner, and there is no match to officiate.
- He is **not a line judge** for the baseline or sideline, for the same reason.
- He is **not a ball boy/ball person**, a coach, a player waiting to go on, or a spectator who wandered down.
- He is not there for any tennis-related function at all; the tennis facility is simply the rented venue for a campaign event.

## Confidence

The footage is low-resolution (854×480), shot from a distance in poor light and badly shaken, so his face and any badge or earpiece are not resolvable, and I cannot tell whether he is private campaign-hired security, venue/event staff or a plain-clothes UCPD officer. But the identification of his *role* is solid: his dark suit, his fixed post at the court corner, his stillness, his orientation toward the audience instead of the stage, the ring of identically posted men around the same empty court, and the uniformed police cordon visible outside the gates all point unambiguously to crowd-control/protective security.

# Answer

The man sitting on the chair in the near corner of the tennis court is a **sign language interpreter**. His purpose is to translate the speaker's words into sign language (American Sign Language) for deaf and hard-of-hearing members of the audience who are seated in the stands nearest to him (the stands the camera is filming from).

## What the video shows

- The event is a night-time political rally, not a tennis match: a "RON PAUL" banner and podium sit on the far court, the speaker is at the podium, and the stands around the courts are packed with spectators. The near court is kept empty except for this one man.
- He sits alone on a white chair at the corner of the near court, dressed in a dark suit, with his **back to the stage/speaker and his body turned squarely toward the crowd in the near stands**. A spectator or security guard would face the speaker or stand; he is placed so that people in that section can watch him instead of the distant stage.
- While the speaker is talking (roughly 17-28 s of the clip) his **hands are continuously moving in the space between his chest and his chin**: they come together, separate sideways, rise to his mouth/chin, drop back to the chest and change shape from moment to moment. He is not holding anything; the light-coloured shapes at his chest are his bare hands against the dark suit. Frame-by-frame stabilised motion measurement shows the movement is concentrated at hand/chest height, not at his head or legs, and both hands move independently (at times clearly apart from each other), which rules out an object like binoculars, a radio or a camera.
- When the crowd is cheering at the start of the clip, and again around 29-31 s, his hands are lowered and resting together in front of his lap, i.e. he pauses when there is nothing to interpret and resumes signing when the speech continues.
- The dark suit against which his hands are easy to see, the fixed seated position in front of a specific block of seats, and the constant gesturing toward the audience are all standard for an interpreter provided at large public events so the event is accessible to deaf attendees.

So, in short: he is not a security guard, umpire, or spectator; he is the event's sign-language interpreter, seated where the deaf/hard-of-hearing section can see him, signing the speech to them in real time.
